title: Scoring methods: movieola, film counter, click track
summary: He used a clock rather than click tracks.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: The one that I remember most in Mickey One, it gave you the impression that more than usual the music was being directly with an integral part of the movie.
Did they go through the standard practices of giving you a reel and saying put this on the movieola and write the score accordingly? Or was there more give and take between you and the producer?
There wasn't that much, and there was very little with the guy I worked with on the coast. He didn't

say a word. Sometimes I wished he would. He must have had enough experience to know that it's better to let somebody go. There were directors also who gave all sorts of rope; I prefer that, although it makes it sometimes easier if they tell you what they want, even though they don't know.
I did have to go to the movieola; at that time I had never done one before. I didn't know how to do it. All of a sudden, it's by you.
So I called a neighbor up here who used to conduct Movietone News which caused my breakup with Hershey Kaye, because Hershey can't stand it, or couldn't.
He conducted the movie for me; I conducted the record, but he did the movie.
Yes, because he knew how to get around that time thing.
They didn't use click tracks then. They weren't around. That all came later. It was known, but they didn't use them in New York.
We had what was called a film counter, but I would write the thing for so many seconds and he would watch the film counter and when--you know, make sure they landed where they were supposed to.

But even to write it, how to stop it, when you want to write it and if you don't know that stuff you have a problem. I still have a relatively unorthodox way of scoring because of that. I do better with a clock than I do with click track.
Click track drives me crazy. I had to use them on the coast, but it makes it very mechanical, a terrible sound comes out of that.

You have to. They prefer it now because they get through faster, they don't have to spend so much time in the studio that way. Everybody likes it better; certainly the entrepreneurs like it better. So you're pretty much forced to use a click track. If you try not to, the acoustics in the room foil you.

I tried not to out there and I couldn't, because nobody could hear you, either my stick is not clear enough or they're not used to following it anymore. It was all over the place and the only way to bring it together was the click track. That didn't happen in New York, but the engineer has a lot to do with that, how he places people.
